utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, The Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted, Alex Demirdjian, for the Prosecution, with Case Manager, Thomas Laugel, and our intern, Simona Onicel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Olmsted, you wanted to make a submission before the witness comes in.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And it's with regard to 65 ter 5127, which was the last exhibit I showed the witness prior to completing my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we have it on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yeah, it's -- it's 5127.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, our submission is that this is -- well, first of all, it's a letter from the British Medical Association to General Kadijevic and it's dated 9 December 1991, and we can see from its contents its primary concern is a significant number of persons, patients, and staff who were missing from Vukovar Hospital after its fall. And it is our submission that, first of all, this is a letter addressed to a named JCE member. And it's significant because the head of the SSNO Security Administration and a direct subordinate to General Kadijevic has testified that not only was he not aware of this letter, he was not aware of the information contained within it, and so we believe this is evidence of failure to act upon information that was available to the JNA leadership. And it's also significant that the witness has testified that, had he been informed of this information, there were concrete measures that he would have taken. I should also note that the witness was also able to confirm some information in this letter. For instance, the letter does speak about Vesna Bosanac and other doctors, and the witness has confirmed that Bosanac and other doctors were in detention at the collection centres and, in fact, the day after this letter he was involved in an exchange of Ms. Bosanac with the Croatian authorities. In addition the Trial Chamber has received into evidence subsequent correspondence from other international organisations or NGOs with similar content. And I draw the Trial Chamber's attention to P2643, which is a letter from Helsinki Watch US dated 21 January 1992. And if we could just briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And for those reasons, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And for those reasons, Your Honours, we make the submission that this document may be tendered into evidence at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, as regards this exhibit, I can see the name of Veljko Kadijevic, General Veljko Kadijevic, of course, and according to this letter, he would be the head of the SSNO, but I also see something handwritten in this letter which would indicate that General Kadijevic was the head of the armed forces. Is that the same position or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I think that's a good question, Your Honour, and I think in layman terms, it is. The head of the SSNO was, in essence, the commander of the armed forces. He was subordinate to the SFRY Presidency, but certainly in times of conflict, and the Defence counsel may correct me if I'm wrong, certainly in times of conflict, the head of the SSNO was, in essence, the commander of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would object to the admission of this document. First of all, there is no nexus between this document, the content of this document, and testimony of the witness. He clearly testified that he has no -- anything about this document, about the content of this document, and it is reason because I object to admission [microphone not activated] this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Zivanovic, isn't that the point that Mr. Olmsted just made? The fact that the witness says he doesn't know anything about it, is the -- is the -- the link that, if I understand Mr. Olmsted correctly, that he is drawing between the addressee, General Kadijevic, and the -- and -- and -- and the author of the document - pardon me - in other words, that it is -- that in it the ordinary course of events, having regard to the witness's position it is something that ought to have been brought to his attention and the fact that he says it wasn't is the -- is foundational to Mr. Olmsted's application. Did I misunderstand you, Mr. Olmsted?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You understood me perfectly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is my submission that it is not enough for admission of this document, Your Honour, because something that was sent to General Kadijevic as a superior to the witness should not be known to the witness. It is not necessary to be known to the witness. And because of that, I -- I -- in my submission, there is no nexus for -- between his testimony and this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The majority, Judge Mindua dissenting, decides to overrule the objection. The document is admitted. And please mark it, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document shall be assigned Exhibit P2974. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, General Vasiljevic. Sorry for the delay. We had a procedural matter to address. Mr. Zivanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: During your testimony, you spoke, on page 7890 of the transcript, that -- about Velepromet as being the TO centre in Vukovar, if I understood you well.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean a reception centre?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I guess.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I used the term "reception centre" because there was some captured persons there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who established that centre?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was getting information -- or, rather, I got information from that -- about that centre from Captain Borisavljevic, the security organ, in 1995 or so when he told me about where some prisoners were, who had to be transferred to the barracks pursuant to some threats, and he was speaking about the TO being in charge of that centre. But I personally never went to Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that yourself, on a number of occasions, mentioned --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the end of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see P2285.2284.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a report which was sent to the Security Administration on the 10th of November, 1991. I think it has already been shown to you, but we'll go through it once more. You see that it says, I'll start with the second paragraph. It says: "A centre for the admission of civilians and preservation of material goods, Vukovar, Jug south has been set up within the offices of Velepromet, which is directly managed by Srecko Borisavljevic, captain first class from the security organ of the Guards Brigade, our first mechanism for finding extremists and possible disguised member [sic] of the MUP and the ZNG." Was that information known to you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Security Administration got it, but it doesn't mean that it reached me. However, I cannot contest anything you've just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It goes on to say: "The head of the centre, Ljubinko Stojanovic, businessman from Petrova Gora, who is otherwise a security organ source, who was given detailed instructions for work on security matters when he came to Belgrade." Do explain to us what "source" means here.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every person with whom the security organ speaks is a source. However, we must distinguish between sources and collaborators.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of instructions were given? What were these instructions mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It goes on to say what is done in connection with identification and the rest of it. I'm going to show you some other documents that have to do with Velepromet. Do you know, did you ever learn from anyone that only such people could be released from Velepromet who were under the control of the security organ, that that organ was the only body that did -- did that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I've already said, I know what Captain Borisavljevic told me in 1995. He clearly pointed out that this is about material assets, war booty, and it all stayed in that centre. And, secondly, Borisavljevic, of all persons detained and screened as possibly having committed war crimes, had to be transferred to the barracks for their even safety. When they were leaving during the final operations on the 19th or 20th, I don't know, Ljubinko stayed behind. And all the time when I was talking to him I had the impression that he was a member of the TO and that's why he stayed behind. Now, who he went to see in Belgrade and why, I don't understand. They could have prepared him right there. There was a security organ, Sljivancanin, and so on, and Borisavljevic himself who had been in the service quite some time. Now, I cannot say any more about this. I only know what he told me in 1995 and on the basis of that, I gave evidence. And it's important to me that they were transferred. When there was a danger for them, because Arkan was there, then he transferred the people to the barracks in order to protect them, which means that he had a group of people for whom he -- he was in charge of them, operatively. But he certainly wasn't in charge of everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: He told you that he transferred some people from Velepromet to the barracks because, otherwise, they would have been in danger.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see D81, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a certificate which certifies that Marko Crevar was authorised by the above command to take over two prisoners from Velepromet in Vukovar, and I believe that you can see who signed it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The signature is illegible but since he is a major --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, well, this could also be enlarged. At any rate, we can tell that the person in question is a major. I think that the printed name is legible too. But why am I showing this? It follows from this, as far as I can tell, that not every prisoner could be taken out of Velepromet without a written approval of the security organ. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this doesn't says "Velepromet." It says "unit command, Negoslavci." And there is no security officer here. Well, if you can tell me who signed this, I cannot --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But the name is printed too. Perhaps we could enlarge it some more.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it could be Veselin Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And, as for a Velepromet, I believe that the last sentence mentions Velepromet. At any rate, we can move on to another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, D82.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here we can also see some dates when the takeover took place, the 20th of October and the 21st of October, 1991, respectively. They were used for some digging work. Did you have any information to the effect that people could not be handed over from Velepromet without the approval of the JNA organ in charge?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what is doubtful here. If the army detained some persons, then it was in charge of those persons. If somebody wanted to take them over, they needed approval from the -- the officer. And if that's how they proceeded, I don't see a problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Exactly. There was a procedure concerning captured persons who were handed over to someone that their names had to be noted down and a note had to be made about who they were handed over to, so it had to be documented.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the collection centre at Begejci was in existence, and it was natural that those deprived of liberty or detained after the screening, these persons had to be sent to a collection centre if their processing required more time. That depended on the Chief of Staff, the chief of the 1st Army, and the corps commanders, so this order was passed down to corps command level. They had a reception centre here, but what became of it, I don't know. I never went there. When I was in Vukovar, I wasn't aware of it. If I had known, I certainly would have gone there to see the place. But what could possibly be a problem with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, there isn't a problem with this at all. I only showed you this document to confirm the existence of a procedure in place in the army at the time. If there was a hand-over, be it to other military authorities or civilian authorities, a document had to be made about that hand-over which people were concerned and so on?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if it was a permanent hand-over, but if the people were used for digging, that was a temporary hand-over and in that case it wasn't necessary to note the names. It's a good thing that they made such notes at all, in such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, you know, I didn't know that it was unnecessary to write down names and surnames. People can go missing, for instance, and then the commanding officer of a unit could be held responsible. After all, there should be a document that says that someone is then responsible for their further destiny.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what it says here, and if they go missing, then he is going to start a procedure in terms of who are the four persons missing, for instance. But it is a good thing this was noted down so there was some kind of control over this, after all, so they were not just locked up and squeezed into a detention space and nobody ever cared what happened to them after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I wanted us to see, Exhibit 532, according to 65 ter. This is also a document that the Prosecutor showed you during your examination on Monday. I think it is on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we zoom in a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, I'm actually interested in the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we please have a reference. We cannot find this passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. No, no, it is the last paragraph of the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "In order to more realistically assess own force, particularly in the field of combat morale, we acquainted the chief of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, cabinet, with the content of the operations report. He expected -- he expressed a certain amount of surprise and at the same time he expressed a degree of reserve at the objectivity of reporting by the Guards Brigade command." Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now that I am reading this, on this page, this has to do with the existence of Serb volunteer groups even as entities and even requests that these units be given a special task, the organ, security organ did get certain directions, but all of this goes beyond our possibility, so I really need to see what this is that Vuk Obradovic is reacting to. Looking at the regulations, and we did discuss who this information went to and I mention who was superior to who, so the Guards Brigade was then subordinated to the command of the 1st Military District. Vuk Obradovic does not have any command responsibility in terms of the brigade, while it is resubordinated to the 1st Military District. And they are informing him, too. And then he is providing his own assessments but he is actually not out in the field so he cannot decide on that, and he cannot really change anything. From this, I just see another detail, that the security organ is subordinated to its commander. I assume that that is Lieutenant-Colonel Djukic, the chief of security, at the office, the cabinet, and he does give this to his superior officer but he does not have any possibility to change anything. This expression here, "he was surprised." I really don't know what that would mean, what he was surprised about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in something else now. Since this report was sent to the Security Administration, and that can be seen on the first page, I think.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would be interested in the assessment provided by the Security Administration, in terms of this report, and whether you know about that, in terms of its authenticity. Let me just tell you something else. It says here also that this report of the security organ of the Guards Brigade is attached. However, we don't have that attachment.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it can be seen up here what the reaction was to this report. It says here Lieutenant-Colonel Mojsilovic; that is to say, these are tasks for Lieutenant-Colonel Mojsilovic. And now this is the handwriting of the chief of the 1st Division at the Security Administration --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not catch the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So one should not have any interference from the Security Administration. This has to do with archives. Assessments, I don't know, cabinet SSNO, probably chief of security regarding the situation in the battalion of the military police. That's probably correct. Now that Vuk Obradovic is surprised, that has to do with the situation in the battalion of the military police. As far as I can remember now, yes, it is on the first page here, there are things that are said about Zjajo Muris and the anti-terrorist company. And Vuk Obradovic is surprised by Zjajo Muris's behaviour and the behaviour of the people from the anti-terrorist company. Now what kind of problems they had, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. How do you know that he is surprised by Zjajo Muris and not surprised by this information?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he knows who Zjajo Muris is. I would also be surprised to learn that Zjajo Muris did something bad. I do apologise. I would be surprised if Zjajo Muris appeared now in some new light, if you will, and this anti-terrorist company that was an elite unit, I'm convinced that this note of Vuk Obradovic had to do with this, what I've been speaking about just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you believe that he was not surprised at all by the fact that from this report -- actually, I don't know how true that was, that prisoners of war were being killed?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't even know that that's contained in there. Actually, I'd have to sit down and read the entire passage. If you have enough time, I can read it passage by passage and give my comments. I did not have this document before. This is the first time I see this, and now I am interpreting it on the basis of my own knowledge about the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness's memory needs to be refreshed. If he can be given a paper copy - I have one here - maybe he can just look at it briefly, as I know that this was shown to him during direct examination, and I don't think he has put the two documents together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What -- what exactly did you give to the witness, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This is just the -- the original version of the document that's on the screen. It's a two-page document and Defence counsel was referring to something on the second page, and I think just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Now I can enter this polemic. What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There's no need for a polemic. I had put a question, or rather, you provided an explanation what -- as to what Vuk Obradovic had been surprised at. You've already provided answers to that. So would you perhaps like to add something to that answer?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was surprised by these observations too. In relation to the Vukovar operation, Serb nationalist and Chetnik propaganda is assuming serious proportions. So in terms of its breadth it considerably exceeds the participation of volunteers and paramilitaries. Nationalist symbols, nationalist songs, speeches by Vojislav Seselj are being tolerated, and that is understand justified. We are indicating this tendency that there is tacit recognition of the legitimacy of Chetnik officers, the existence of Serb volunteer groups as establishment entities and even requirements that such units be given special directions and tasks. In preventing such phenomena, the security of the brigade received some guidance but broader measures are required as well and that exceeds our abilities. So he is indicating these other problems as well, this other group of problems. Now what was Vuk Obradovic surprised by? I think, primarily, by the officers from the anti-terrorist company. Now whether he was surprised about this too, I assume that he had received information about that as well, these problems in the combat zone with volunteers, Seselj's speeches in Vukovar. But I can only make assumptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Briefly we can finish with this document now. You hadn't seen this report, this document, at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that it did reach the Security Administration but what was stated was that it should be archive, that no measures should be taken.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because it was Vuk Obradovic who was really in charge of this. And also the organs for morale and political education. That's what it was called at the time, and it really does have to do with the morale of the unit at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, P2001.1981.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the report that we already looked at several times. You know about it, the 10th of December, 1991. Can we move to the end of this report, the last page; that is, paragraph 8. In paragraph 8 of the report, it is stated: "The reception centre ... functioned successfully (Velepromet) and about 9.000 to 10.000 men, women, and children passed through it." So I conclude on this basis that the security organ was in charge of this centre, since this report about the work of the centre is being submitted by the security organ.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. Major Sljivancanin is writing a final report. This is not a separate report about the reception centre in Velepromet. Less there be any misunderstanding, in the reception centre that Major Borisavljevic told me about, there is this information that we saw here, about 200 to 300 persons, and then 25 were selected. So I would like to remind you of that centre. This is a reception centre. That is what it was called. What happened on the 18th, 19th, and 20th, when the operations were over and when the population was being taken out of cellars, destroyed houses, et cetera, and then they passed through this reception centre. That is the reception centre and the time when -- that Sljivancanin is silent about, when they tried to kill Colonel Vujic, Bogdan. That's that centre, not to have any confusion. That's the month of October, in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to tell us that there were two reception centres there, at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could just say that these two centres have nothing in common, so it is Velepromet but the activities are different. In the reception centre from the month of October that the Guards Brigade was in charge of in relation to persons who were brought into custody for some reason, there were about 300 persons there, as far as I can see from that information that was looked at here. And, secondly, there is this centre, the reception centre, through which the population that was leaving Vukovar passed through. Sljivancanin is giving a very rough estimate here from 5- to 10.000 persons, 9- to 10.000. Whereas, in Sremska Mitrovica according to the information of the Red Cross, 5.000 persons had passed through there. And then there was speculation that there were 5.000 or 10.000 persons at the reception centre. Not true, 2.600 and I don't know how many. So this is a rather one-sided, rough estimate. The most interesting thing is that he did not describe key matters in this report at all. And that is what happened to the persons who left Vukovar, who were evacuated for -- from Vukovar and who interfered there? And how the officers who wanted to introduce order in that centre faired. He says nothing about any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you read this report now, I would like to know how you can conclude, based on this report, that there are two separate centres?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now that you're showing me this document, telling that there were 9- to 10.000 people and trying to persuade me that this was a centre headed by Borisavljevic. But Borisavljevic had to escape from that centre because it was assaulted and he had to evacuate the people to the barracks. He couldn't do that with 9.000 people. This is the first time I'm drawing the conclusion that when he says "collection centre," he means a place where people were taken because, from there, they were transported to a place of their choice. Once again, this is not the collection centre for prisoners of war under the control of the brigade and in -- in October and of which Captain Borisavljevic was in operative charge. And they had to transfer the people from that place and evacuate them further. That was done, evacuation, and not detention and processing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And this centre, through which 9- to 10.000 people passed as we read here, was not under the authority of the security organs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke about the establishment of civilian authorities and said that a distinction has to be made between the establishment of civilian authorities at Lovas in October 1991, on the one hand, and the activities pursuant to the instructions of the SSNO when bodies for civilian affairs were established and, as a consequence, Town Commands. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to focus on the first part, and the second part will be discussed later. Let us talk about the establishment of civilian authorities before that instruction from late November or early December 1991. Please take a look at paragraph 9. It says: "There was progress in organising and forming organs of the people's authorities and police stations in the zone of active -- the zone of combat activity." From this, I conclude that OG South was forming civilian authorities in its zone.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably we must distinguish between OG South and the Guards Brigade. He doesn't mention the Guards Brigade forming and information of, and so on and so forth. He says forming. I would say providing assistance. I don't think that they appointed the president of the municipality or whoever. You said that you had information that he was the one who appointed that man, Ljubinko, I forget his name, a TO commander who replaced Dusan Jaksic. I wasn't aware of that. He probably understood it to be his duty to do that. And as far as I remember, around the 18th or 19th of November, upon the cessation of combat activities -- and I forget the date of that instruction that was sent out containing the tasks of the Town Commands and the assistance to be provided in the establishment of authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I seem to remember that it was subsequently, in late November, and the tasks were assigned on the 6th of December. But we'll get there yet and discuss it in more detail. Please take a look at paragraph 10 of this same document. It says: "The Gmtbr security organ bore the brunt of the work in forming those authorities, organising security and safety measures, and receiving and processing prisoners."

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I think that's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. That's what I wanted to clarify.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Organisation of security and safety measures in the combat zone is in the charge of the command and its security organ. This is a well-known thing. But if you're alluding to the establishment of civilian authorities, I don't know if they were establishing them or assisting in the establishment, and I don't think that you know either. And I have already said that I was dissatisfied with the language he used but never said what the security organs did, what the results of their work were, and what came out of the questioning of, say, those 25 who had been screened as suspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying that this was in the purview of the security organ or your purview and that you were supposed to do anything about it. I just want to know or make sure that this is a fact mentioned in this report where he says that the security organs bore the brunt in the forming of local authorities and providing safety for the reception and processing of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, paragraph 47, if you want to take a look, you spoke about the tasks of the JNA or the three stages the JNA went through from the start of the armed conflict until the end, and you said that, in the first phase, it was the JNA's task to separate the parties to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me now which these parties were according to the JNA? On the Croatian side, I suppose it was the national guards corps, the ZNG or their MUP units?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And what were those forces on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The self-organised forces that armed themselves. And that's how the conflict arose, because it was all happening in the territory of the Republic of Croatia. They were claiming that they were the legitimate authorities there and treated them as rebel groups, and that's how the conflict began.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The armed Serb groups, what did they want, really? Did they want to remain in the same state - that is, the SFRY - or did they have other ambitions? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, certainly I do. Above all, they wanted to protect their rights that had been taken from them when the HDZ came to power. The Serbs were a constituent element in Croatia and they were turned into a minority without the rights that a constituent people had. That's the essence why there was dissatisfaction among the Serbs. Until the month of March and the Presidency session I have mentioned, the order on the disarmament of all paramilitaries was in force. That did not apply only to such units in Croatia but there were also similar units in Kosovo, Sandzak, and elsewhere. From the month of March onwards - and that session did not result in the proclamation of a state of emergency in the country - the Serbs who until then were poorly armed, they had procured arms through individual channels, had hunting rifles, and so on, turned to President Milosevic for help because the Croats did not return their weapons. They only returned 427 pieces of armaments and they had imported 18.000 AK-47s. And then Serbia began assisting the self-organisation of the Serbs in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please slow down because I believe it was not said how many weapons were returned.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can elaborate. The Croatian side returned 427 weapons of which only ten were automatic rifles, Kalashnikovs from the Hungarian contingent. However, the Serbs, after the -- issuing of the order of the president of the SFRY on disarmament, and it was first and foremost the Serbs in Knin, returned the weapons that they had and removed three roadblocks that they had set up, because that was the order of the Presidency of SFRY. Since the Croats did not disarm, the Serbs considered themselves tricked, and that's why they applied for help to Serbia, among others, help in arming themselves. Up until then, they had their own local armed units who had hunting rifles or whatever they had, and they could be found mostly in the villages where there was a majority Serb population. This may not be directly related, but it will be related to Borovo Selo. The Croatian authorities started setting up police stations in places where there hadn't -- there had never been any, and those were mostly places inhabited by Serbs. Secondly, at police stations, where mostly Serbs lived, they would conduct raids mostly at night and take out weapons from the reserve police force. I believe that there were 18 such stations. This all irritated the Serbs. It wasn't so much connected with their desire to stay in Yugoslavia, but the more -- they felt threatened and that's why they started to organise themselves. And as of March, as I mentioned, they were growing stronger because they were able to procure weapons, behind which process there was Serbia. Now the question arose, if all Serbs wanted Yugoslavia. Some did want to stay in Yugoslavia, but there were others who didn't want to stay behind in other republics; in this case, in Croatia. That's how the motto became popular, all Serbs in one state, and then people started speaking about Greater Serbia. Some political parties were founded, and the Croats -- the Croats who lived there but weren't a majority were supposed to move to Croatia, if they wanted to live in Croatia. And when did the establishment of the TO begin in Slavonia, to be specific? I don't have any exact information about that. I know that autonomous provinces began to be proclaimed. It started with Knin. And others followed their motto, in Slavonia and Srem. And then there was the incident at Pakrac, when Croatian police officers were disarmed and a Serbian police station established there. Later, there -- there was an attempt to do the same at Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You say that you don't know when the Territorial Defence was established in the territory of Croatia. However, you said that these village guards existed, if we're going to call them that, these people who guarded their villages, protecting them from possible attacks. We have quite a bit of information about that too. It was based on a principle of self-organisation, wasn't it, of people from those villages? Is that the way it was?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the first stage, that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So during this first stage, as you say, they did not have - how do I put this? - a single command? Everybody guarded their own village?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the question is what the first stage is, what period that is. That is the period of the end of 1990 and the beginning of 1991. However, in Pakrac, political leaders emerged. They started working on the organisation of the Serbs. There was this national council or whatever they called themselves, and they practically guided all this activity in that organisation. They established contact with Belgrade and with people in the government of Serbia and directly with Milosevic too. And there was this attempt through retired generals who hailed from that area to establish contact with the JNA. So this does show that there was some organisation. The JNA, in the Krajina, tried to establish a system of Territorial Defence. I've already said that plan, unity, from 1987 disbanded military units in the territory of the Knin Krajina, Lika, Banja and Kordun, and then the SSNO ordered that activity be initiated on bringing these units back. There was this order from the SSNO that had to do with the establishment of these units. That is characteristic of the Knin Krajina. The Territorial Defence started being organised and in what form in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem? I cannot say right now what the exact date would be and what the exact period would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that you said Western Slavonia and Srem, whereas, the record says the opposite. All right. Later, when this organisation of the Territorial Defence started, as you said, this Territorial Defence actually included these members of these village guards, these units that were in the -- there in the beginning, that were practically self-organised. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would assume that this would be the natural sequence of events. They were self-organised and then the organisation came. Weapons, arrived, institutional links with Serbia. So all of this assumed an organisational nature. Since we are talking about that, these clashes between the National Guards Corps and the MUP forces, the ZNG wanted to establish their own authority in their territory and then there was the self-organised Serbs. And then later on, they were organised in some form of Territorial Defence, so these clashes started. And then the JNA was called in to intervene, to separate them, to prevent clashes, and then was attacked by the National Guards Corps and the MUP, and, truth to tell, sometimes by some Serb units which did not want these activities to go on. They did not want the Ustashas, as they said, to be protected. So they did things as suited them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you have any information during this first stage, that is to say, practically before Croatia officially declared its independence - that was on the 25th of June, 1991 - are you talking about that period now or are you already in July, for instance, these early stages of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These conflicts in the area that we are discussing went on without interruption. They went on in August too. There were clashes that occurred in August as well. From September onwards, all-out blockades started of army barracks and that's when the JNA got involved in the de-blockade. That is what General Kadijevic spoke of in his book. So this was not done in a planned fashion, namely that up until one month this will go on, and so on and so forth. The operations became more extensive and more intensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since you often -- since you said that often the -- the opposing sides did not like this role of the JNA and that sometimes they would fire at them, either one side or the other side. Tell me, when the blockades of the barracks started, was it both sides that blockaded the barracks or only one?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If we are talking about Slavonia, Baranja, Western Srem, no, Serb forces did not block the barracks. However, we did have a case in Bijeljina where Arkan's unit blocked the barracks so that they would not intervene regarding what was happening in Bijeljina. I think that was in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us just clarify this. This is in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In these efforts to de-blockade the barracks, did the JNA manage to carry that out in some of the barracks and how successful was it in that effort?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depended on the resistance put up and also the persistence of the units involved. So the situations were different. The barracks in Vukovar was blocked already in August 1991. Let me not repeat everything that is already contained in this statement. The 14th of September, when they sent a dramatic dispatch that they had been under blockade for already 20 days, that they had no food or water, that they have fatalities, they cannot bury their dead and they have wounded persons who they cannot treat medically, and then General Kadijevic established contact with the European monitors in Zagreb, asking them to convey this to Tudjman and to make it possible to de-blockade the barracks and to enable the transfer of the dead and wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about that extensively in your statement. I just wanted to ask you why in this specific case the JNA allowed for one of its barracks to be under blockade for 20 days and that their people basically had no -- bare living conditions. Why did they wait for 20 days before they took concrete action?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This action led to war, which did follow. The SSNO did not allow for them to be under blockade for 20 days. They probably had the opportunity of submitting reports about the situation because before that, considerably before that, commanders were issued the following order: That small facilities should be abandoned and that units should be kept in larger facilities that can defend themselves, and that there should be sufficient, water, food, medical equipment, generators, power generators, and so on, so that they could defend themselves. The army was in favour of an alleviation of the situation and resolving problems in the country peacefully, to have them resolved by peaceful means, not by military force. Now, there are different situations. The command of the Varazdin Corps had surrendered after two days of blockade, whereas the brigade in Bjelovar stayed on for another seven or eight days and continued to fight. And the corps command had already surrendered and withdrawn to Belgrade, and some brigades stayed on and fought. Some remained under permanent blockade, without surrendering.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now that you said this about these brigades, these units that stayed on and fought. Could you please tell us when this decision was passed not to defend small facilities, to concentrate forces in larger facilities and to have sufficient food and water supplies, medical supplies, et cetera, if barracks were to be attacked?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it must have been March or April 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Another thing, at the time were there any plans for action if these surrounded garrisons in some territory could be de-blockaded, if we can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the commanders who were in that situation expected some help to come from the outside and they did not draw on all the resources that they had. Usually they asked for air force to be used. The general position was as follows: If you are attacked, defend yourselves by all means and respond even more than necessary. So they were not prohibited from defending themselves. But this was a specific situation. This was a situation when fire had to be opened at a town where people lived, people that you lived with, communicated with, so this is not a classical war. That's why there was a great deal of caution, and commanders gave this a great deal of thought, whether they would apply the force that they did have and how they would do that. Resistance was put up to the extent possible, rather than firing with artillery at neighbouring buildings. So small arms were used, and quite a few people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does this look like some kind of hopeless resistance if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I note the time. If it is a very short question, it's okay. But if not --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, very short question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Doesn't this look like some kind of hopeless resistance? If these surrounded garrisons are defending themselves, irrespective of the resources they have, if they do not receive any external support it is as if they were doomed to die?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. They were supposed to hold their facilities as they were and it was the political echelons that were supposed to resolve matters. That is how the situation would have been resolved. When politicians did not resolve the situation, then the rest started.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: General, it's 10.30; time for our first break. Thirty minute, as always. Court Usher shall escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one second, Mr. Olmsted. I have something to deliver as well, a very short oral decision. We are seized of the Prosecution motion for replacement of page 30 of Exhibit P1418, with a revised translation of that page filed on 30 August 2013. Would the Defence wish to make any submission on that -- that motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber hereby grants the motion, and the Registrar shall take any necessary action to implement the decision. Thank you. Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. With regard to the two documents that are included as associated exhibits for this witness's 92 ter package that Your Honour raised yesterday, this is 65 ter 2491 and 65 ter 2929, the problems with those documents have been resolved and loaded into e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Sorry, I forgot to ask pending of document 1D656 into evidence. It is the order of 10 October 1991 about the attack on Lovas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If I recall the only thing the witness said was that this is what the document says. I don't think he provided any substantive evidence regarding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it's enough he spoke about Lovas -- Lovas -- whole Lovas case and role of the army and the role of the TO Valjevo and the role of Dusan Silni volunteer detachment. So I -- I think that's enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, is your intervention meant to be an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: On the grounds that this witness really wasn't able to speak to the document, other than to say what was read to him is what is said in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We'll come back to your request and -- and -- and the -- the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, in your statement, in paragraph 48, and you may take a look, you said that you were present at a session of the council for the protection of the constitutional order on the 30th of June, 1991, where Borislav Jovic addressed the session, and he said then that no one should be forced to stay in Yugoslavia and that if the Slovenes didn't wish to do so the JNA should withdraw from Slovenia to new borders. Do you remember that? Of course, he did not mention what those new borders, where the JNA should withdraw to, were. In that same paragraph, paragraph 48, or a bit lower down, in fact, that would be paragraph 51, you were shown two articles, newspaper articles, two exhibits, and you said that in both those articles, Goran Hadzic spoke about the expansion of the borders of the area of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem and a mutual exchange of populations. I would like to show you this article and to ask you something about this issue of the expansion of borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see Rule 65 ter number 310, please. [Interpretation] Perhaps we can zoom in on the B/C/S version. [In English] Could you zoom in, please. The text -- text on upper left side of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a text dated the 20th September 1991 that you mentioned. I don't know how well you can read the text, but I know that you were shown this by the Prosecutor. And let me just say briefly that nowhere in this text was I able to find any reference to the expansion of borders of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, so I would like you to take a look at it and tell me if I'm right.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he did speak about Osijek where he mentions Osijek, where he said that Osijek has not been liberated yet for the time being. And that is in reference to the border of the SAO up until then. I don't know what your question is really.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, my question is: Where did you find that? Because what you said in your statement, and you said that you stood by the statement, where did you find in this article that he was talking about the expansion of borders?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, where the reference is made about Osijek and that Osijek has not been liberated yet but that it would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, who says that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he does. You can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me read it then. So it reads as follows, I will read the whole paragraph: "'We are aware that those borders will depend on our forces,' Hadzic said, 'although we are in favour of a democratic resolution of that issue.'" The text is not very easily legible, my apologies: "In response to an American reporter from the associated press to the question whether Osijek was within the borders of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, Hadzic briefly replied, 'So far Osijek has not been liberated.'" And you understood that to mean an expansion of borders?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. He said so far it hasn't been liberated but there were constant efforts to engage Osijek and to include Osijek as part of the area which did not materialise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you said there were later efforts, whose efforts?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the efforts by both the leadership and the Territorial Defence of SAO Slavonia, and there were attempts to put -- to exert an influence on General Biorcevic who had been issued strict orders to ceasefire and not engage Osijek. But I don't know what your question was regarding the first part of your quotation of Boro Jovic's words. You read that out, but I can't see that in the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned that in the context of the borders that you were talking about. But we will get to that. We are still discussing that issue.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to say right at the outset that the context is not the same. If I may --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Boro Jovic spoke twice, addressed the parliament twice at the sessions where I was present, the one that was mentioned -- that you mentioned of 30th June. If I'm not mistaken, that was the 18th Session of the Federal Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order. And the first time he addressed this forum, he said that the army should withdraw from Slovenia to the new borders and only four days earlier on the 26th June at the same session of the Federal Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order when the decision was made on the movement of the army into Slovenia, he was in favour and he called for firm action and that the Yugoslav army should take up the borders and defend them. So this was just four days later where he said something quite different. In other words as Ante Markovic would have said he was not really consistent. But even after that, he was within the Presidency of the SFRY, but no command was ever issued for the army to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that and I will put some questions to you about that. Now you understood this, in other words, to mean his demand for the expansion of borders and you say that there was pressure exerted on General Biorcevic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, this is not what I said. This is what you are saying now with respect of what is written in the article. There was no pressure but there were efforts to engage Biorcevic in activities against Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So there was no pressure?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was called upon not to stop but move on towards Osijek and then he would say, Well, Kadijevic is -- he provides the strategy and I'm supposed to be a tactician and take care of the tactics, so --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter kindly request that the witness repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please just repeat your last sentence. I believe you said that all activities ceased.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, if it wasn't recorded, I can repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So Biorcevic under the influence of the situation that prevailed in the Territorial Defence units, that the -- the -- the engagement should not cease, that they Sid move on against Osijek, in contravention of General Kadijevic's order that all engagement, all of Osijek should cease, I believe that at one point he even briefly engaged in some operations. But when General Kadijevic was informed of this, following that, all activities ceased. So there were calls for moving on against Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's exactly what I was going to ask you about, and we can find this in paragraph 173 of your statement. In this paragraph, you say that General Biorcevic stated, If we would not advance, if we were not to advance, those behind us, the men of Goran Hadzic, would kill us from the back.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that might amount to the pressure that you were asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, could you then now, please, tell us whether you really considered that some of Goran Hadzic's men would go behind the units of the Yugoslav People's Army and shoot them in their backs if they refused to move forward? I mean, does this statement seem feasible to you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not what I said. I didn't say that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Gentlemen, may I remind you not to overlap and to respect pauses between questions and answers in order to allow the interpreters to finish their interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was not the person who made that statement. It was Biorcevic, and it was recorded as his words. So I cannot really interpret what it was that he was trying to say there and what the situation was. I don't know whether he was just trying to be offensive or whether he knew something and that the situation was, indeed, such that if he were to stop they would open fire at him. But, generally, there was a lot of criticism at the time by -- by Goran Hadzic as well at the expense of the army, that it hadn't really accomplished the task it was supposed to accomplish, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: General, could we please leave the criticism aside. There were -- there was criticism from all parts and we can discuss this, if need be. But, here, what we see are threats because this would be an open threat if an army is being forced to move forward and engage in fighting or else there would be men going after them and shooting them in the back. So let's not divert the conversation to criticisms and other matters. What I would like you to tell us is this: As a security officer and the top person in the security organ, you were responsible for protecting the army against such matters as well. For instance, people threatening to shoot them in the back if they weren't to do what they wanted them to do. So I would like to ask you whether you launched any investigation to check this, to see whether it was indeed true, whether there were these threats of this nature, or did you just file this away?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can perhaps now remind you of the ambit of our work, whether this was something that the security organ was supposed to do. You're trying to put this in a different framework. My first question would be, was there any reaction from the government circles at a statement of this nature, to ask him, What are you saying, man? And then there should be a question to the federal secretary, We are not threatening anyone and yet you are threatening to shoot us in the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did Biorcevic tell that to the government or to General Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who he said it to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But then how could the government react?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you see that things appear in the media and people talk, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But, at any rate, do you know if any measures were taken to discover the persons who would allegedly shoot soldiers in the back unless they did what they were expected to do? Specifically in this context, these men of Goran Hadzic's making the army attack a town. Do you know whether any investigations of this kind were launched?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us -- let us go back to the texts about exchanges to some extent. You said that in this text there's mention of an exchange of population. Let us look at that part before we move on to the other text. Here, among other things, an appeal to those who left Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem is mentioned to return. And Goran Hadzic also says who is being appealed to. In other words, only Serbs or others as well. You can read it, if you want. But you said that this is about some sort of exchange of population. And, as far as I can tell, he answered in that context that this appeal also applied to Croats returning; in other words, whoever had left with the exception of extremists, as he termed them. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree with everything that you said. Apart from this article, what does he advocate?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You know something? You gave a statement about this article, and I'm interested to hear whether that can be found in the article. Let's not go beyond the framework of this article, for now.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So in this article, he advocates an exchange of population.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this article?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, do show me that.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People from Rijeka and Pula and wherever should move to Osijek. I'm not reading it now. I'm now speaking from memory. And those who were colonised and taken there by Pavelic will be given return tickets. If not in this article, then in another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, it appears to me that there might be some confusion by the fact that paragraph 51 of the statement refers to two separate articles, and the Defence counsel is focussing on this particular article with regard to both issues, and the witness, obviously, his evidence is with regard to both articles. So perhaps if Defence counsel shows him the second article, this could be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The paragraph 58 -- 51 of -- of the witness statement clearly stated that in both articles Goran Hadzic spoke about the western borders of SBWS and of the exchange of the population. And I asked the witness for this specific article, whether he spoke about exchange of the population or not. And I'll -- I'll also confront the witness with the -- another article.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I think this is really getting down to semantics but I think both articles have to be read together or shown to the witness together for him to give a full explanation of how he perceived events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's not about the events, Mr. Olmsted. It's about the content of the article, whether -- whether something is in this article, or in the other, or not. So I think that's something Mr. Zivanovic can explore with the witness. I think it would be best you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- repeat your question, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down a little bit, please, the B/C/S text.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whether this text speaks about an exchange of population.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We see a headline in both letters. The heading over the photograph: Return of the men. And there it says that return tickets will be given to those who were brought there by Pavelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean in this frame with the headline: Return of the men?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who were colonised in our province by Pavelic during the war from Herzegovina, Imotska, Krajina, and Zagorije will be given a return ticket.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. But that is not an exchange of population.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. It's an expulsion. Yes, I made a mistake when I said "exchange." It's an expulsion of population. In this same text, which is about who was -- who had prisoners and you were claiming that this was the army in the context of Velepromet, whereas Goran Hadzic says here: Hadzic without a customary introduction answered a number of journalists' questions, and the TASS reporter said right at the outset, Although his government offered 20 Guards Corps members taken prisoner in exchange for the Soviet journalists who went missing, there is -- he has no information about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no problem about discussing prisoners and anything else, but do limit your answers to the questions that I asked because our time is also limited. I wanted to clarify paragraph 51, about the borders and Goran Hadzic's wish to expand the borders of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. But let me ask you something else. In September 1991, which borders did the JNA -- was the JNA facing?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The borders of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, the JNA was no longer present in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was. I will slow down now. They had their warehouses, they had armaments, and under the Brioni Agreement, there was a considerable time-period for the stay of technical teams to maintain those assets. And then a decision was to be taken when the JNA would finally leave Slovenia. In September, we still had JNA members in Slovenia. It was not all -- it was not all of the JNA but, as far as we were concerned, Slovenia was still part of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But what about Croatia? Was all of Croatia still considered to be a part of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in Yugoslavia all the time, until it was internationally recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, on the 20th of September, when Goran Hadzic wanted to expand the borders of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, as you said, that's a sin, although it's still part of Yugoslavia, according to the conceptual frame work of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't understand the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, we need the witness's answer, if there was any.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the question was out of context -- or, actually, please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the last thing you said was not part of the context -- didn't -- didn't belong in the context of what we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see document from Rule 65 ter list, 306.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we start dealing with this, you said that the JNA - and I'm referring to paragraph 49 of your statement - that the JNA -- if the JNA had wanted to take and retain Slovenia and Macedonia by force, it could have done so. In other words, it -- it withdrew from those republics voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question isn't well phrased. That the JNA didn't defend Yugoslavia because it didn't want to. It acted upon the tasks as assigned by the Presidency of the SFRY. Let me return to the March session. Had the Presidency ordered the use of the army, then the outcome of the overall situation would have been different. So don't speak about the -- the desires or the willingness of the army as if Yugoslavia broke apart because the army wouldn't act. There was no political will to use the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we do this, could the Defence counsel refer me to whether it's on the Prosecution's exhibit list or the Defence exhibit list? Because it is very hard for me to manage my documents without knowing where it is. And I cannot find this on either my list or the Defence's list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is on our -- our exhibit list -- I'm not able at this moment to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What is the document number, Mr. Zivanovic, the 65 ter number? Do you have that one?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I know the number of document from the Rule 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What is the number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Pardon, sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The document is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No, but I'm looking -- I'm trying -- 306. There is no 306 in your -- in your document list, the Defence exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. In that case, I'll withdraw this document and not put any question to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if I may just ask as a service to the Prosecution, if Defence counsel could refer us to the tab numbers, that's something that I really made an effort during my examination-in-chief. And it really helps us out because by the time the document is called up and by the time I find it in one of my binders half the questions have been asked, and I haven't had a chance to look at the full documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I agree that the tab numbers are very useful to find the documents quickly. I agree with you, Mr. Olmsted. Please proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do my best to find it, but, unfortunately, I did not organise it appropriately.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Among other things, you spoke about the arming of the Serbs in Croatia, and you said that, in 1990 or so, Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, was captured while he was smuggling arms to Krajina. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the MUP of Serbia was behind that.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said something else. We can check what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you -- you -- do say what you said.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP of Serbia took part in the creation of conditions for Arkan and two others to be released from detention. The minister of the interior of Serbia and his Croatian counterpart were in contact, and that tells us that the MUP of Serbia was really behind Arkan's activities. The same applies to their talks about the release of Goran Hadzic, who had also been detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that General Biorcevic issued a false certificate that Arkan was under the JNA.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We must be precise here when you quote my words. I didn't say that he issued him a false certificate that he was under the JNA. He issued him a false certificate about belonging to a recon group of the Novi Sad Corps that was deployed to the Badovinci area for special tasks. That's what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when that was?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, in March, before the events at Bijeljina, in 1991. I apologise. 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me show you Exhibit 2473 from the 65 ter list. It is our exhibit. I see that it's on our list, but I don't have the serial number of the document, unfortunately. Therefore, I'll ask you to look at it. It's on page 75.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Page 95, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a text that was published a while ago in that newspaper, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do we have an English translation of this --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, I didn't say. Yeah, the text has been translated, as far as I know. And we have -- I'm not so interested in the text but in one document published in this text. It is in the mid of this page. If we could scroll down a little bit. This is document -- may we scroll down, please, a little bit more. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I'd like --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And I have translation of this particular document. It is 1D769.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we zoom in a bit, the B/C/S text, so that you can see it better. So it's a document, actually.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could it please be enlarged a bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, right now. It says here that pursuant to the rules on military service and the rules on work of -- and I don't know what this abbreviation is: "I hereby approve the appointment of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan," and then his details, "as commander of the newly established Special Purposes unit under the direct supervision of this organ. "Pursuant to the same rules, I hereby appoint Dusan Bandic ... as his Chief of Staff." And then there's signatures and stamps. I'm interested in the following: Did you know about this document?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a forgery. I categorically assert that. This is not General Marko Negovanovic's signature. This is not the form in which a chief of administration addresses someone, so -- what is this written down here in the stamp? What kind of "uprava," administration is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Political or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
