utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please zoom in on the stamp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What's the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There's no date, at least I haven't seen one.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is the arrest of Arkan, what we've been discussing, Marko Negovanovic was not chief of the political administration then. He was chief of the Security Administration, and I was his deputy at the time, and at that time I was in Zagreb. This is a forgery that was published by some newspaper. You didn't even say which newspaper and we're going to know straight away whether it is a tabloid and whether it's part of a campaign that was waged against the JNA. It's pure forgery. I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My understanding is that this is a Croatian newspaper. We can take a look and see which newspaper it is. This material was probably secured through Mesic, as far as I can see, from what is on the Prosecutor's list.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no need for us to deal with this forgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would ask to tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, well, I think the witness's testimony speaks for itself. But we don't have a date on this document. We don't know about the authenticity of this document. We don't have a translation of the article in which it appears. Really, there's absolutely no basis for tendering this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As for translation of the newspaper article, it could be marked for identification. But I think that the date -- the -- the -- the lack of date on the document is not the reason for not tendering this document here. And I don't know that it is accurate to say that -- that it is false document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, for instance, Your Honours, I see the date in the document. It looks like it -- it's talking about events in 1990, which is well in advance of our indictment period. And, again, the date does matter as to what this document is and whether it's authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The indictment includes the arming of Serbs in Croatia, and in this context, the Prosecution included many allegations and many evidence about the arming of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, another -- another detail. Isn't the relevant thing -- the relevant element not whether it is accurate to say that it is falsed -- forged, sorry, but the fact that this witness states, it is this witness's testimony that it is a forgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's it. But I think that the other document might -- might change his mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We will deny your request to admit this document, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we see document from Rule 65 ter list, 6050.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an order from the command of the 12th Corps, or, rather, a document from the command of the 12th Corps. What is referred to here are the units that participated there. If you look at paragraph 8 - could we please zoom in on paragraph 8? - he says in the 12th Corps we have the Baranja TO detachment, 388 military conscripts, and then volunteer TO detachment consisting of conscripts from Novi Sad, Backa Topola, Smederevska Palanka, total 310, and a volunteer detachment of Arkan's, 70 military conscripts. This was a document that was sent to the command of the 1st Military District. Does this indicate that this detachment, Arkan as it is called here, was within the 12th Corps of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This could just be some kind of evidence of this detachment taking part in the operations of the Novi Sad Corps, as mentioned here. But it could have been part of it only during combat operations. If I may explain this further because I cannot just state it so briefly. From the 1st Military District, why would the Commander of the 1st Military District issue an order in January 1992 to Colonel Petkovic to draw Badza's attention to the fact that Arkan's people are still out in the field? Why did he not give a -- an order to his direct subordinate, the corps commander? It is well known that later on he kept advocating that volunteer units should be formed in the military because they keep deserting from the army. That is a well known extremist point of view of his.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. This is a document, as far as I can see from the very beginning, it has to do with manning level of that unit. And I see here that what is mentioned, inter alia, is that we have - that's what it says - we have the following volunteer units from the 12th Corps.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We'll have a look at the date. I think it's December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Scroll up B/C/S document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 12th of December, 1991. As far as I know, there were no war operations at the time, no combat operations at the time.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is that request that goes back to the 24th of November, asking to regulate the status of volunteers. They will either stay in the JNA or will be expelled. That is that order of the Presidency from a date that we know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just one thing. I agree with what you said. On the 12th of December, he is actually saying what his situation was at the time. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is trying to show Arkan as if he is an element that should be kept, that he is in contact with, that this is a legal unit, and the way he lifted his arm, look at the wounded hero, and so on. The question was how the 1st Military District reacted to this kind of information. Even little children know that Arkan was not part of the 12th Corps. Now what he wrote, whether he had to account for it later, that is something I don't know. But I claim that he was not within the 12th Corps, outside combat operations. And to what extent he took part in that, too, is a separate story all together as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm told that it is already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And it is also included in this witness's 92 ter package in the statement at paragraph 94.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Exactly. May we see, please, Rule 65 ter 6019.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an order dated the 30th of October, 1991, again from the command of the 12th Corps. This is an order for some combat action. And, again, in paragraph 2, there's a reference to tactical group Vihor and the units are listed there that are included in that group, including the territorial detachment of Borovo Selo; volunteer detachment, Arkan; then Luzac; then two detachments from Serbia; then companies from Trpinja and Brsadin Territorial Defence, this is Slavonia and Western Srem; then Kole volunteer detachment; and Mandic. And they are given a certain task there. Do you agree that these units were under the command of the 12th Corps at this point in time, the 30th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that that is the way it is written here, but to what extent they were actually under his command and control, that is something I cannot assess. However, some volunteer detachments, I -- I mean, the names themselves are telling: Kole, Mandic. That tellingly demonstrates the situation that existed in the 12th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would check whether this document was tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is. It's P1685.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you. May we see P2715.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is General Panic's statement, as given to the OTP. [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Two issues with regard to this. First, as the procedure is that if it is in fact a ICTY interview, Defence counsel should have refrained from identifying the person who was being interviewed. And, secondly, I am not certain what this is. Even though I'm certain that we disclosed it to the Defence, it is unclear with regard to who took this interview, who this is an interview of, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This document was admitted into evidence and there is no confidential mark on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: According to our list --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Objection withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to see page 25 of the English text. In Serbian, I believe it's page 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, while we're calling this up, I was speaking to my colleague here, and it's my understanding that this is not an ICTY interview. It's a BBC interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry, maybe I misunderstood that it was interview given to the Prosecution. Sorry. But that's better if it is to the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's just be fair and say at this stage it's certainly not an ICTY interview, given it's -- the way it appears. We don't -- we believe it might be a BBC interview. We don't have the video to confirm that. But that is what is marked on our data. But the source is still a little bit unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's a Prosecution exhibit now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's admitted in -- into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah. As Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, and I'm not raising that issue. It's just as far as identifying where it comes from, it's a little ambiguous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah, Mr. Zivanovic's qualification of this document as an ICTY interview was --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe it is not accurate. I cannot say it right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if the part I'm interested in has been found in the Serbian version. At any rate, I believe we have it in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll read out the text in English because I cannot see it in the Serbian version. And it will be interpreted to you: [In English] "I think the operative units did their job correctly, but the mobilised units were not prepared adequately for action. And when you don't prepare them adequately, you have -- you encounter the problems that you just mentioned. And that's how volunteers started appearing and we trained them for action, for combat action in Belgrade, and they were fighting together with our units. They included Arkan's Tigers and Seselj's Chetniks. They were not big groups, say, in Arkan's case between 80 and 120 persons, and in Seselj's case between 90 and 120. All these formations were under my command. But the people who wanted to act independently were being removed from that area and disarmed and returned home." [Interpretation] Based on this, my impression is that General Panic, as commander of the 1st Army District knew that Arkan's and Seselj's unit were under his command.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's what he says, then he would probably know. And it is not an issue whether or not they took part in combat activities. But later on, he wanted to get rid of them and couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, 1D617. Would you zoom in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an order. And I see that in the upper right-hand corner it says Colonel Z. Raznjatovic personally. There is a reference to the Law on the Armed Forces, and it says "Order": "Make a breakthrough on the Bijeljina-Loznica-Visegrad axis while moving out the Muslim population, regardless of casualties," and so on. It is not dated either, but most probably this is probably 1992. And we see that it is signed by the chief of General Staff. Does this mean that Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, was under the command of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This, again, shows that this is a very clumsy forgery. Let me substantiate. We see how this was drafted. Not even a non-commissioned officer would have drafted such a document, let alone that the General Staff of the JNA would do that. And the stamp is blurred again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We can blow it up.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It again says "political administration." Where did you get these?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The OTP found it, not me.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want to show this as being a forgery, great. It says chief of General Staff but the stamp reads "political administration." And it's the same stamp as in that article that was -- where General Negovanovic allegedly signed the -- the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No matter who came up with this document. This is a forgery. If the OTP has military experts, well, the least you could expect for them to have is a pair of glasses like me to take a better look at the stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you're saying that this is a forgery?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: General, even if the two documents are forgeries, which I don't know, but you say that they are, there are some statements here and other documents that show that Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, was under the command of JNA units; that is, the 1st Military District, and the 12th Corps respectively. A great number of reports were shown to you, submitted by security organs about various criminal acts, alleged crimes committed by Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, and that group of his that was out there. And I also noticed that basically no proceedings were launched against him or his men. Since these reports were written by the security organs of the 12th Corps, for example, was this engagement of his in -- in the framework of the 12th Corps a reason why no proceedings were launched against him? Instead, reports were being written.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an additional proof that, in reality, he did not belong to the 12th Corps. And the security organs knew full well what this man was like, who he was. I'll will not mince my words. The drunkard, General Biorcevic, said -- and he is a good man but he has one little short coming: He drinks a lot. And he as a drunken fool comprises both himself who is a general of the JNA by raising Arkan's hand to show that he was wounded in the finger. Did I act upon that? On the 28th of October, 1991, I contacted the minister of the interior and the chief of state security to tell them what Arkan was doing on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It seems that you misunderstood my question.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whose business it was to take measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I asked whether it was a fact that the security organs of the 12th Corps merely submitted reports instead of filing criminal reports. Do you think that the reason for that was the fact that he was engaged in combat activities, or whatever activities of the 12th Corps, and the 1st Military District?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was the other way around. If he had been part of the 12th Corps, they may have been in a position to file criminal complaints or -- or inform the corps command of that man's activities. How can he be part of the corps if he had his base at Erdut? How can he belong to the 12th Corps if he wants to enter the command of the 12th Corps forcefully and slaps a policeman on the face who didn't allow him to enter? And then a lieutenant of the military police raids Erdut to see what Arkan is doing to one of his soldiers, and since the captain drew his weapon faster then the guy said, Okay, okay. How can he be a member of the 12th Corps subordinated to the corps' command if he has his own base, has his own training, and kills people at will. I cannot agree with that. You can show whatever documents you want. He was being used in these actions because it was convenient. Whoever is willing to fight, let them fight. But -- but in -- in documents, it seems that he is some sort of unit of the 12th Corps because those documents were written by trained officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we should come back after the break to that very last answer. It is a little bit confusing to me. General, second break. We'll come back at 12.45. The Court Usher will escort you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Olmsted. About -- about 1D656, the Defence tendered, and Mr. Olmsted objected to. The objection is sustained. The witness, indeed, didn't say anything else but the document said. So the objection is sustained and the document is not admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, just to clarify with regard to Exhibit P2715. I apologise for my ignorance. It is not shared by the other members of the team. I've now learned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The ignorance, you mean? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The ignorance is not shared by other members of the team. And I've now been able to clarify that that is indeed an interview by General Panic. It's the raw footage of an interview that what was conducted by BBC back in 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Now, the little query I had about the last -- about the witness's last response just before the break. Let me see whether I can find that. Yeah, there it is. Is my -- my confusion or my doubt shared by anybody? I mean, what -- what -- what the witness seems to have said -- what you seem to have said, General, is: In documents it seems that he," and we are talking about Arkan, or Arkan's people, "that he is some sort of unit of the 12th Corps because these documents were written by trained officers." Is that what you meant to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And I can perhaps explain that, clarify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document, this is a military document properly put together. There are tasks assigned, and it is noted there that the Arkan's unit is part of the 12th Corps. Then I tried to explain that, in factually, or actually it was not part of the 12th Corps so then I explained that it -- that this unit had its centre in Erdut and not within -- or on the premises of the 12th Corps, then that a policeman would not let him enter the premises of the corps, and then that there was the slapping of the policeman. Now there are other arguments that I could put forth to support what I'm saying. On the 20th of November, 1991, at Velepromet, there was a session of the regional government attended, among others, by Arkan. Mr. Hadzic introduced him as a guards commander, or something like that - it's just a paraphrase - at the Territorial Defence that had just been established within the region. Now, this was on the 20th of December. As for the information that Arkan was a member of the 12th Corps, it dates 12th of the December. So this is not really logical. As a member of the 12th Corps it wouldn't be logical for him to attend a government session and be promoted by the prime minister as a person who was part of his Territorial Defence. That's number one. Now also in all the footage, video footage that you see, you could always see that he never wore a JNA uniform. They had some special uniforms and they did not bear the same insignia that the JNA soldiers did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. I perfectly understand your arguments to say that he was not a member of the 12th Corps. But what I do not quite understand is that you -- that you say that from documents, it looks like if he is member of the 12th Corps, and the reason why it looks like that is - that's what you say - is because these documents are written by trained officers. How would trained officers make documents that look like if he is member of the 12th Corps after everything we heard -- hear from you to underline that he wasn't?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is not contentious that he took part in combat in the area of the responsibility of the 12th Corps and that at time he had, as it said there, 70 men in his unit. General Biorcevic wanted to create conditions for him to really be -- to really become a part of the new Army of Yugoslavia, to draw him in. I saw a couple of documents, I was shown a couple of documents by the Prosecution, where he set forth his reasons why all volunteers should be treated as members of that future Serbian army. And if I may use that term, he kept trying to legitimatise him, to present him as someone who was subordinated to the command, including Zivota Panic, and under Zivota Panic -- and when I said that this document was properly put together, what I meant was that they didn't really discuss whether he was actually a member of that army. Biorcevic was the person who assigned him to be in his own corps but he was actually never a member of the JNA, and he never had the rank of Colonel, as we saw in that falsified document. He just proclaimed himself to be a colonel and he also appointed a deputy or something of his.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, General. That's very helpful. Mr. Zivanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the last thing I asked you about had to do with Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, and the information that was forwarded by members of the security organs relating to various -- alleged crimes committed by him and his men without actually any proceedings ever being taken against him. Now, you mentioned an attack or assault of his, that he assaulted a military policeman or a guard or something like that, and I believe that you spoke about that in your statement. But could you tell us now, talking about this assault on this military person, was there -- was there -- were any proceedings instigated against him?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a criminal report for assault on an military person in the course of his duties. Now what the outcome was, I don't know, but the criminal report was submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There's another thing that I would like to clarify. In a number of reports submitted by the security organs that you were shown by the Prosecution, next to his name I did not notice that there was ever mention of any other member of his unit who allegedly committed these crimes, so -- and there were also no crimes mentioned specifically. Now, can you tell me what was the reason for sending such reports?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we have specific information about his crimes in Dalj, and there's also an Official Note of the duty police officer at the time regarding this event. He was, for all practical purposes, under the protection of the MUP throughout this time, and the only real commander who could issue orders to him was Radovan Stojicic, also known as Badza.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to move to your description of the Vukovar operation. You talked about this in your statement. You also said what you knew about it, and you also testified about it in these proceedings. First, I'd like to ask you this: If I understood you correctly, you were in Vukovar on the 19th of November, 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What part of the day was it, approximately? Was it in the early hours or later hours, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. On the 19th of November, I attended a meeting in Milici in Bosnia and Herzegovina which lasted the whole day. It was a meeting with the republic MUP members and the federal secretary for national defence, General Gracanin. In the evening on my way back from this meeting, I was informed by my deputy that the Vukovar operation was over and he proposed that we should meet on the road as I leave Bosnia. From there, we left together and arrived at around 1900 or 2000 hours. I can't tell you exactly what the time was but it was already dark. I did not go to the brigade command headquarters and I didn't know that a group of the security organ was already there. It had been sent by someone, and I can only guess who might have sent them, probably the chief of security of the 1st Military District, to Vukovar. Now they reported to the brigade commander in order to offer their assistance in the triage and evacuation of the civilians who were being pulled out of the town, the buildings that were pulled down, and these three or four retired officers who were recruited at the time by the 1st Military District security organ, they communicated directly with the brigade commander. Now my presence there was limited to my knowledge on the operation having been completed, some losses, if there were any in the course of the day. We talked about the fact that a group of prisoners, I think from Mitnica - I'm not sure if it was the 204th Brigade - had been send to the collection centre in Sremska Mitrovica, which had been established there. I didn't stay there for a long time. I saw Marin Vidic then and asked Sljivancanin what he was doing there. I mean, I can go into these things, but I don't know if I need to. I ordered them to immediately send them to Mitrovica and I think there were two other persons going with him. So I returned from Negoslavci from Belgrade, and on my way I stopped in Sremska Mitrovica to see what was going on there and I saw that these people were housed in various rooms, so I didn't really spend much time. There I left for Belgrade. So that's about my stay there. But you know, as well as other people, that there were various things inputted to me, that I was allegedly the one who had sent these officers, and so on, although I had nothing to with it and I didn't know anything about what happened or what was happening that night and the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: During the time while you were in Vukovar on the 19th November, could you tell us, if you recall, which officers of the 1st Guards Brigade you met there, any officers that were there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I didn't meet any other officers other than Major Sljivancanin, the security organ, also other officers from the security organ, Vukasinovic, Karan, and other security organs who gathered when they heard that I had returned. They were joyous. They wanted to share a drink with me and so on. I stayed there briefly, and I was really looking at and interested in them collecting the necessary documents and reports, and I -- because they were in those parts, I wanted to make sure that they didn't run into land-mines or something like that. So I did not contact any other officers that evening, other than these people that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you about their plans for a the following day? What it was that they were going to do, what their tasks or assignments were, whether they had received any assignments from their commander or any other task that they would have to do as part of their duty?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I've already told you, it was an informal meeting. They just said that they were happy that the operation was over, that they had survived it. And there wasn't much talk at all about any future activities. All that happened was that I learned that there were people taken prisoner. When I asked them what happened after the operation was over, they said that this Mitnica Brigade had surrendered and that their men were sent -- had been sent to Sremska Mitrovica. And then on my way back to Belgrade I just stopped there briefly to see whether they were accommodated properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you that officers from the 1st Military District had arrived there, these retired officers from the security organ?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that they did not know it themselves because I think that there was some 200 metres away from the headquarters, the brigade headquarters. These men were about 200 metres further, in another building, and they never mentioned them. And I'm sure that at that time while I was there and throughout that time they did not know that these men, these officers, had arrived. And had I learned it from them then I would have asked to meet with them as well. However, they were exclusively on the premises of the brigade headquarters, and I'm sure that these men, including Sljivancanin, didn't know that they had arrived because, had they known, they would have told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see that you mentioned them in your statement, that, on that day, they were in Vukovar, and I thought that that was when you learned that they were there. Can you then tell us now when it was that you learned that they were there on the 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know that they were there on the 19th until the instigation of criminal proceedings before a military court in Belgrade when they appeared as witnesses. And then we talked in the hallway, we discussed this. Now, as for what was happening on the 19th and all the events there, as I've told you, I learned it about it then during these proceedings. Now as for when I learned that they had been reactivated it was when I went to that meeting at the collection centre, I think on the 13th of November, where I met with a military prosecutor, which is when I saw that there were some retired officers who were members of this team of the security organ. Now because at the time I -- there were --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter kindly asks that the witness repeat the last part of his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: General, the interpreters did not get the last part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I learned that these officers were reactivated, recruited by the security organ of the 1st Military District when, on the 13th of December, in 1991, I went to the collection centre in Mitrovica where I attended this meeting with the military prosecutors. At the time, there were active security officers who were not deployed anywhere because they had been withdrawn from Slovenia and Croatia. I felt that it was not necessary to reactivate retired officers and then they were withdrawn from the active service, and they returned to the collection centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know, then, how it was that these retired officers then happened to be in Vukovar on this date, on the 19th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They received orders to come to Sid. They were in Begejci at the collection centre there. The chief of the 1st Military District, General Babic, was waiting for them there. They were in Colonel Petkovic's office, and from then they were given the task to go to Vukovar and help deal with the situation, evacuation, and so on. So, from Sid, they went to Vukovar and went to the brigade command. They went to see the brigade commander. When they completed this effort, they returned to Sid and met up with General Babic again. After that, they went to the collection centre. As far as I managed to find out later, they did not compile any documents as to what it was that happened on the 19th, 20th in Velepromet, in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, or, rather, do you know how come they actually happened to be in Sid? They were in Begejci. You concluded that there was no need for them to be involved any longer because there were regular officers who were not busy at the time so perhaps this is a strong word, but you let them go. You dismissed them?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: General, could you please repeat your answer. The interpreters did not get your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please start from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Begejci, from the collection centre, at the request of General Babic, they came to Sid, where the operations group was of Colonel Petkovic, and he was waiting for them there. And from there, he sent them to the Guards Brigade and to help with the evacuation of the population that was underway. On their way back from Vukovar, again, they went through Sid. As far as I learned from them afterward, General Babic was waiting for them there, again, and from there, they went to the collection centre in Begejci.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So they did return to Begejci from there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you were returning from Vukovar, did you have contact in Sid with any of the security organs there, either General Babic or Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not stop in Sid at all because I was busy all day and I was in a hurry to get back to Belgrade and I needed to have enough time to be able to go to Sremska Mitrovica, too. So I didn't stop in Sid at all and I did not talk to anyone either from Petkovic's group or anyone from Sid at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you wanted to stop in Mitrovica, you said that these prisoners were in dormitories. Did you go to that prison in Sremska Mitrovica, or did you go to some other place?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the KP Dom and I was escorted by their policemen to the area where these people had been put up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You went to Vukovar again, I think you said on the 21st of November, and that was your last visit to Vukovar during the war-time-period. So when you went then, were you in contact with any of the security organs from the 1st Army? Babic or Petkovic, that is.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not in Vukovar on the 21st of November. My statement maybe says that it was after the 21st of November. It could have been around the 25th of November. Why? Because the Guards Brigade returned on the 24th of November. And I did not contact anyone there, and there wasn't anyone there that I would get in contact with. I was sent from the General Staff with General Vuletic, chief of the intelligence administration, and I had my deputy with me, General Tumanov. So we went in connection with a particular problem that had probably reached the operations centre of the General Staff of the JNA, and that is that a group of volunteers there was making trouble. They didn't want to return their weapons, and they didn't want to leave the area. I came to this group. They were pretty drunk. They reacted to the fact that they were not given any certificates about participation in combat in order to be able to get financial compensation. After a relatively short conversation they calmed down and I explained to them how they could receive that. And the problem was resolved. It was raining very hard and I returned to Belgrade straight away because that is what I went there to do. That was the task that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you didn't have any contacts with General Babic or with Petkovic, starting from the 19th of November. We're not interested in previous contacts. From the 19th of November onwards, you did not have any contacts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to these retired security officers, do you remember how many of them there were there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps eight to ten. That would be my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember their names?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would be quite hard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did they include active-duty officers in that group that came to Vukovar on the 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think NCO Korica was there. And I'm not sure whether Captain Dragan Muncan was there too. I was reactivated in 1999, as you know. Before that, I hardly ever had any contact with officers from the service. And then, after those seven years, I had an opportunity to ask what it was that had been going on, and I know from then that Korica and that Muncan were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When did you receive information -- actually, first of all, did you receive any information at all, why it was that they were sent to Vukovar on that 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that up until that testimony because soon after that, after what we have been discussing just now, I was pensioned off and I did not have any contact with people from the service then. I was in contact with them when criminal proceedings were instituted before the military court, and I talked to them then and that is when I heard that they were there. And later on, through different trials and testimonies, because the trial was re-started before our courts and over here, that's when I found out what it was that happened then and who was where. But none of them told me what it was that happened concerning the execution at Ovcara. In my statement, I said that when I had my first information that something had happened in Ovcara that was in 1993. And now let me not mention who it was. I talked to Captain Borisavljevic after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you find out from this contact with them or in any other way what the reason was they were sent on the 19th of November? Why were they sent there? Why was this officers of security organs sent there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To help the orderly transport of these persons and initial selections that were supposed to be carried out, who would go to the collection centre, and who could be released to go wherever they wanted to go. So they were supposed to help in this situation, in this commotion, help from their own point of view, because these were experienced officers, colonels, lieutenant-colonels, and that's why they reported to the brigade command, not to the security department at Sljivancanin's.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that they were supposed to carry out some kind of selection among these people who were there in Vukovar and they were supposed decide who was to be sent where, I mean, whether they could freely go to Serbia or Croatia or whether they were supposed to be kept there as POWs or something like that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My conclusion was that this kind of selection - objectively - could not be carried out because of the situation in which the population was gathered there and taken further. Then Sid. Then Mitrovica. The Red Cross of Serbia was involved in taking in these people in Mitrovica. And the security organs had to deal with that, and they were supposed to assess who was supposed to go there, but there were persons who had been taken prisoner who were wearing uniforms and who had weapons. It's the entire Mitnica Brigade that was there and they were disarmed in a classical, military, soldierly way. No selection was required there. These first contingents that arrived were rather well-known people. We -- there was knowledge as to who these people were. They were wounded. They went to the collection centre, so it was only logical that they had taken part in combat activities. Later on, various organs from the ground were non-selective, the military police, the police, the military. Some persons were being brought into custody - sorry about this - and sent to the collection centre. In documentation, I found out that some had been beaten up before having been brought to the collection centre. They had been beaten up by the police, milicija, and then the leaders of the operation teams reacted and told the MUP people not to do that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, on the 19th of November, this group that surrendered at Mitnica was transferred without the participation of the security organs at all. I mean, the security organs who were sent from Sid. Perhaps it the security organs of the brigade itself that took part in this.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because when I arrived and that team of the 1st Military District was at the brigade command, so when I arrived, I already knew that this Mitnica group had been transferred to the collection centre that had been established in Sremska Mitrovica. So that is to say that they had left, so these four or five officers could not have taken part in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to our information, according to my information, at least, on that 19th of November -- actually, for the 20th of November, what remained was the evacuation of people who were at the Vukovar Hospital. I don't know whether there was any other place involved because basically all the other Croat units had been disarmed and the one from Mitnica, too. Does that mean that they were supposed to carry out this selection at the Vukovar Hospital to separate the people who would go to Mitrovica, that is to say, perhaps to this collection centre, from the people who were supposed to be allowed to go wherever they wanted to?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not give any assignments with regard to this selection when I was there. Later on, I learned from trials and from other things that happened, they were given an assignment by General Mrksic, these four or five officers who came. That evening, I didn't even know whether the hospital had been evacuated or not, so I did not go in, and I had no idea who was left there. I heard of this Mitnica Brigade ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is what I'd like to ask you, perhaps a bit more specifically. Later on, when you discussed the matter, did anyone tell you what specific task they were given in which selection they were supposed to take part, and whether they were supposed to take part in the transportation provided for these people?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on I saw that there was an order issued by General Panic to evacuate the hospital. Because I see that there were some people there from that organisation, doctors, who were providing help, et cetera. I suppose that they were all supposed to be sent to civilian-health institutions or elsewhere in the territory of Croatia. I can only make assumptions now. But I see that Major Sljivancanin was around the military hospital and that the military police were securing the military hospital, that Colonel Bogdan Vujic and others from that group from the 1st Army came there. So they certainly were not there just to watch. They took part in this selection. In 1997 I asked the then-head of the Security Administration to conduct an official interview, not a personal conversation, with Colonel Sljivancanin, he was a colonel by then, to find out what happened in Vukovar and about all of these things that were being said, like in the media, that I had stolen money from Vukovar. And I had that official interview on the official premises in 1997. I'm not going to list all the officers who were present there. He told me then that he had problems, too, when he was getting personnel out of the hospital, not during some kind of selection but for them to go to the next place that they were supposed to go to, a temporary collection centre at Ovcara where the 80th Brigade was. As they were getting them out of the hospital, already then --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please do slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise. When they were being taken out of hospital, he had problems. He had a rifle pointed at his back. It was a TO man who did that. According to list -- who -- a list that he got from Vesna Bosanac, a list of hospital personnel, and he released them, and he was in a situation to almost be shot in the back. In that commotion, he first transferred them to the barracks. That's the first thing he could do because he considered them safe there. But then that group went to the barracks, and problems started there. And let me not go into the details now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When he said that he transferred the people from the hospital to the barracks, did he say why he didn't take them to Mitrovica immediately?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go into such subtleties. According to their procedures in place from before, he was to take them to Ovcara. And there the first screening was made, who would be released and who would be taken to a collection centre. Since there were problems in front of their hospital, the TO men wanted to snatch them already. Then he fled to the barracks with them. Actually, he sheltered them there. If there hadn't been the barracks, then he would have taken to Mitrovica, where the 80th Brigade was.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the latter part of his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please repeat the latter part of your answer. I will read out this last sentence that was interpreted: [In English] "If there hadn't been the barracks, then he would have taken to Mitrovica, where the 80th Brigade was."

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke too fast. I apologise. If it hadn't been for that situation, as the situation in front of the hospital when the people were being taken out of there, they wouldn't have gone to the barracks but, instead, directly to Ovcara, which was some sort of a makeshift reception centre, and from there they would have been either sent to Mitrovica or released.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody -- anyone of these people tell you that, or is that your free conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an interpretation of my -- of the interview I had with Sljivancanin on the official premises of the security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you were in Vukovar on the 19th of November - actually, it was Negoslavci - did anyone of the security organs tell you that on that day there had been an international mission that wanted to visit the hospital and that they had some problems with them, a discussion, a debate?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We have information that on that night the security organs really went to Negoslavci and that there was a total of ten of them. Five were from the 1st Military District; and the other five were sent there by the Security Administration. I want to acquaint you with that so that you may tell us to what extent that is correct.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one was sent from the Security Administration. I wasn't at the Security Administration then. I was in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's number one. Furthermore, nobody ever mentioned that to me later. Nobody mentioned that anyone was sent there from the Security Administration. They were only sent by the Military District through Sid, where General Panic waited for them. If you have the names of these officers who went there on the 19th, I might provide further comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [In English] I refer to transcript page 6391 to 92 and page 6430.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I have these names, but I'm prohibited to tell the names to you. Those are our rules. I can only tell you what information I have but not the source of information.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You may want to be careful using that information, and it would have been a good thing if you had been more careful when you received that documents that were forged.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you had some problems with reporting that had to do with General Babic. You said that you noticed that some reports about crimes that you received from Milici Jovanovic, who was your second subordinate, as it were, which reports he sent to his first superior along professional lines and these reports never made it to you. Was that before the Vukovar operation or after?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After. I was speaking about the 4th of December. And around the 12th or 13th of December, I saw General Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask him to send you the -- the detailed reports that he had received from Milici Jovanovic, or maybe make a summary report and forward it to you, about all this information about committed crimes that were never reported to the Security Administration?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you know what the purview is of the security organs, then -- well, you're insisting that we are the only ones responsible for reporting about crimes committed in the territory. The information collected by the security organs about things outside their purview were communicated by them to the officers in charge. Why didn't he forward information received from Colonel Jovanovic to me? He said that this information was forwarded on a need-to-know basis, and that's why he didn't consider it necessary to send that information to the Security Administration, because we're not responsible for such things. Furthermore, Colonel Jovanovic, at the briefing, gave me -- communicated his observations to me, and I didn't need second-hand information about what I already knew. I don't think I need to explain any further, but I can. Babic, for a number of years, was my first superior in the security organ. When I became chief of administration, he was my subordinate. I was careful in the way I communicated with him, because he was older than I was and he had been my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But the information you got from Milici Jovanovic, who, in fact, was subordinated to General Babic because he had a number of security organs in the 1st Military District who were subordinated to him. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Didn't that indicate that information that from other units came to the 1st Army District, also from security organs, weren't communicated to you either?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But much information was received by counter-intelligence, mostly by the 1st Military District because it was a big Military District. But the problems were happening in the area where there was combat, it was the Novi Sad Corps. The Kragujevac Corps had remained in their area. And that's where the problems were, with what you're talking about - there weren't any problems with the corps at Uzice or Kragujevac or wherever - it was the Novi Sad Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I agree that this is not -- it's not exclusively jurisdiction of the security organs to prosecute perpetrators of crime and it's stated in the -- rules of service. But in paragraph 42 of your statement, if you want to take a look at it, let me quote: "If a member of the army committed a crime and the JNA security organ or other commanding organs knew about it, it would be those organs' duty to report the crime up the chain of command."

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chain of command. What's meant here is up until the command. Because I already explained, it wasn't the exclusive jurisdiction of the security organs. I mentioned Lovas. And the organ for political work, Eremija, got information from Petkovic. Petkovic reported up his professional hierarchy to the assistant for morale and political work who was a general, and nobody asked questions to him and his superior what they did about it. And they had the prosecutor's office in their jurisdiction. And now I'm answering these questions as if our service were the only one that there was in the army. We reported about things that we knew to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you received information about events in Vukovar later, can you tell us from whom you got that information or, to be more precise, information concerning the evacuation of people from the Vukovar Hospital? Who informed you what was happening there and how it all went.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody informed me of their own accord. I retired in 1993, and then I learnt about some things from Ovcara for the first time. There were some officers that I trusted because I was no longer a member of the army, and I had been in remand prison, and I was accused and then tried. But I went to -- through these people whom I trusted to inquire about things. And in 1993, I started collecting information and talking to people. The first such conversation with a man whose name you know, I needn't mention him; the second one was Srecko Borisavljevic; the third one, I discovered, was the commander of a military police company, a reserve officer who was then in the 80th Brigade at Ovcara. I informed the chief of the Security Administration of everything I had found out. Nobody ever asked why the chief of the Security Administration who succeeded me in my position was questioned and called to testify. As for the information from 1993 which was requested by Zivota Panic, you will see that the crimes committed at Ovcara are not mentioned there, and I don't believe that they didn't know about those crimes then, more so since some people from those circles were rather close with the leading people in our administration. When I left, General Nedeljko Boskovic, for example, got an early promotion. In January 1998, I was prevented from obtaining some information. I was told literally, Comrade General, stop meddling. I don't know what the purpose of this is, but I'm glad I can speak about this and you know what I was accused of and what I -- and what was said about me, that I had been in agreement with the Croats for 200 people to be killed. The one who threatened me had people from the Vukovar Trojka, with whom he could clear up these things. I was -- and then there was this affair with Mane. I was in remand prison when that was going on, the proceedings. But nobody talked to me about that because they found out that orders were being obeyed. And during that interview with Sljivancanin in 1998, he went to his strong box and took out receipts about money being deposited with the SDK of Serbia. And in my case, amounts of 3 to 5 million were being mentioned, the currency being either dollars or Deutschemarks. But I don't know what this has to do with these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that you have digressed too much. I never asked you about General Boskovic or these other proceedings. I limited myself to your information about the events in Vukovar and at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is all indirect information I obtained, and you know what weight that has.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Another thing: You must have heard about this -- actually you spoke about it, too, this government session in Vukovar, or rather, in Velepromet. In your statement, I think there are two dates, both the 19th and 20th of November. According to your information, were these two sessions or one? And was it simply a -- not possible for you to say exactly which date it was?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, if Defence counsel could refer us to the paragraph in the statement which refers to a meeting on the 19th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I try. I rephrase my question, but I'm sure I'll find it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You talked about a government meeting in Velepromet. Can you tell us -- or rather, do you know when it was that this government meeting was held? Do you know the date?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I saw, after so many years, in different statements different dates were referred to as to what happened when. I am of the opinion that this session was held on the 20th, not the 19th. Why? Because the team that was sent from the 1st Military District arrived in Vukovar on the evening of the 19th. And Colonel Vujic was at the government session. So the session took place on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Another thing, let me be more specific, I think that you talked about Arkan's stay in Vukovar, in that period of time, after the liberation. Can you tell me whether during those days immediately after the liberation of Vukovar, to the best of your knowledge, was he there once or did he come twice?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I just know what I saw on television. When it was broadcast on the news that a government meeting had been held and then there are statements of Mr. Hadzic's when he said that now the Territorial Defence had been formed as their armed force and that Arkan was appointed as some kind of commander of some special unit of theirs. I saw that on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have to tell you, not that we don't have that footage, but according to what I know from my client, too, he never made such a statement. At least not about that, the establishment of the Territorial Defence and Arkan as the - how did you put this? - the commander of some special unit?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, media reports from that period need to be looked into, and you can find it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You saw that on television, you say?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was this on that actual day, when this session was held, this government session, or was it a day later, or some other day before that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was on the news that day. Finally, there are those statements made by the officers who were in Velepromet, from Borisavljevic, Bogdan Vujic, Warrant Officer Korica. They said that Mr. Hadzic came to the government session with Arkan and that threat was issued then. Yes, captain, that's what you're going to do, when he transferred the prisoners from Velepromet to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So one thing is this session in Velepromet, or rather, the fact that then on that day Goran Hadzic was there and Arkan was there. That is one thing. I asked you about the organisation of the Territorial Defence, and that Arkan was appointed commander of some special unit, and that such a statement was made on TV?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You heard about that or did you -- did you see that yourself, did you hear that yourself, or did you hear about it from the people you mentioned a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that I remember seeing that on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It seems that your memory doesn't serve you very well, General. Please, according to your assessment, do you think -- you know who Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, is and possibly what his position was in this war. Would he accept to be - how did you put this? - commander of special units of the Territorial Defence of Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I think we're venturing in the realm of speculation, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I ask just for assessment of General, if he could give it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I could. But I don't know of what value this is for the proceedings that are underway. Arkan gave himself the rank of colonel and the people around him the rank of colonel and different ranks. He enjoyed any kind of promotion. However, that he would be obedient in respect of Mr. Hadzic or anybody else, that's the part I do not believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see the clock, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic. Could I ask you, Mr. Zivanovic, what your planning is? Do you have any indication about how long you need tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how much time I have on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: A little bit more than an hour, Mr. Zivanovic? Would you need that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. 1 hour, 20 to be exactly, but that's only to be exactly, to give the exact time. And then, Mr. Olmsted, any idea about redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm hoping it will only be 20 minutes. But I do believe that, regardless, we're not going to complete the next witness by 2.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Certainly not. That's -- that's far --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Would it be possible to make arrangements so the next witness doesn't have to stay over the weekend, for either extended sitting on Thursday or Friday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll -- I'll first allow the general to leave the court. General, we are finished today. As you could hear, we -- your testimony is not finished yet, so we expect you back tomorrow at 9.00, and, as I told you yesterday, this means that you can't discuss your testimony with anybody, and you can't talk to any of the parties. Thank you very much. The Court Usher will escort you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, if I understood you well, your -- you asked for arrangements so that the next witness does not have to stay over the weekend. Is he already here?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, he is here. Actually, he was ready to start today, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So your arrangement would mean that we have -- we -- we would have to make arrangements this week. Now, tomorrow we would have, more or less, more or less than more, one hour left after the general, right? One hour, 20, let's say, 1 hour and a half for Mr. Zivanovic, 20 minutes for you. That leaves a little bit more than an hour. No? Am I -- am I bad in math? I know that for a long time now. So tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm equally bad at math. It's possible - maybe Mr. Zivanovic can confirm - we may be able to finish during the first session or maybe towards the beginning of the second session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So we have two hours left.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Next witness is a viva voce witness. Estimate three-hours in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. And I have confirmed with the trial attorney who is going to be leading that witness and she expecting two and a half to three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Two and a half to three.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That gives ... two and a half to three hours. Three hours to the Defence. Do you have any indication yet, Mr. Gosnell?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Very little cross-examination expected. But, of course, with a viva voce witness, hard to be precise on these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The suggestion is to have one extra sitting on Thursday afternoon and ask the parties to do whatever is possible to finish at the end of that sitting. Would that be possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I -- I -- I -- I'm speaking perhaps somewhat out of turn, but I do have a suggestion or a way that this might be expedited. We would waive any objections to having the statement 92 ter'd, if that would be accelerate matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll have to check on that suggestion. We appreciate Defence counsel making that suggestion and I could either -- we could probably provide information to your Chambers later this afternoon whether that's a possibility. Of course, that would save a substantial amount of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah. It is -- it is, of course, a helpful suggestion without any position on -- on -- on all the other questions. The only problem for me now is: Do we already ask for an extra session tomorrow, or do we wait for that ... when we know whether it will be a 92 ter or -- is -- do you know, Mr. Olmsted, whether this -- whether this is a viva voce witness because the Trial Chamber refused a motion to 92 ter the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'll have to check on that but my understanding is this was a 98 bis witness and the Trial Chamber rejected that motion but did not, in turn, say 92 bis under, I think, provision (C) or (D), which allows for cross-examination but admission of the statement. And I believe we didn't file subsequent motion seeking 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And when could you take a position on Mr. Gosnell's offer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I think sometime this afternoon. There's -- I will have to speak to Mr. Stringer and, of course, the attorney who is going to lead the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So you would take into consideration that we need to ask for an extra session tomorrow, if -- if we need one, by COB today. We would like to have your information, let's say, at least at the latest an hour before, okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That shouldn't be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And then perhaps you could think about the question, whether if it -- if the witness is 92 ter'd, whether tomorrow morning would be sufficient, right, or would we anyhow need an extra session tomorrow afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I -- my -- my expectation is if we do admit the statement 92 ter, that would substantially reduce the amount of direct examination. And presuming that Mr. Gosnell is correct that he does not have an extensive cross-examination, I don't think that will be any problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We'll wait for your further notice. Thank you. Court adjourned.
